prompt_free_text:
This paper studies a timely and important question in scalable Bayesian inference: when and why Bayesian coresets provide accurate posterior approximations, and what fundamental limits govern their quality. The main contribution is a set of general lower and upper bounds on forward/reverse KL divergence between the full posterior and a coreset posterior, with substantially weaker assumptions than much of the prior theory. The paper then uses these bounds to derive negative results for importance-weighted subsampling schemes and positive results for subsample-optimize methods, and supports the theory with experiments on deliberately challenging models featuring multimodality, unidentifiability, and heavy tails.

Overall, I find the paper technically ambitious and, in several respects, genuinely valuable. The lower-bound perspective is especially novel and useful: the literature has had many algorithmic proposals and some upper-bound analyses in special settings, but much less understanding of impossibility phenomena. The result that importance-weighted coresets require coreset size scaling linearly with dataset size to maintain bounded KL, even after optimal post-hoc scaling, is a strong and practically relevant message. The paper also makes a credible effort to move beyond the standard strongly log-concave / exponential-family regime, which is important for the coreset literature if it is to claim broad applicability.

The strongest aspect of the paper is its conceptual framing. The author argues persuasively that large-scale Bayesian inference should exploit redundancy rather than rely on asymptotic normality or smooth unimodal structure, and that coreset theory should therefore cover models with latent discreteness, multimodality, weak identifiability, and heavy tails. The paper’s examples are well chosen to reinforce this point. In particular, the Cauchy location model with likelihood depending on theta squared and the rank-deficient logistic regression example are not toy cases in the sense of being artificially easy; they are intentionally outside the comfort zone of many existing analyses. This makes the theoretical generality more meaningful.

The lower-bound machinery appears to be the paper’s main technical contribution. Lemma 3.1 is elegant in that it isolates a local overlap quantity over a set B while avoiding direct dependence on the tails of the coreset posterior, which would indeed be difficult to control. The subsequent theorems reduce posterior approximation error to properties of weighted sums of score vectors and Hessians near a concentration point. This reduction is intuitive and potentially broadly reusable. The distinction between Theorem 3.3, which handles “reasonably good” coresets, and Theorem 3.5, which handles poorer gradient matching under weaker global assumptions, is also sensible. The resulting applications in Section 4 are compelling: the negative result for importance-weighted coresets gives a theoretical explanation for an empirical phenomenon that many practitioners have likely observed.

The upper-bound side is also interesting, though I found it somewhat less satisfying than the lower-bound side. Lemma 5.1 is a clean generic inequality, and the introduction of an “(f,A)-subexponential” condition is a reasonable way to abstract moment generating function control for the centered log-likelihood vector. Theorem 5.3 then gives a simple KL upper bound in terms of a quadratic form in w-1. This is a useful perspective because it connects coreset quality to posterior variance of log-likelihood approximation error. However, the practical force of the upper-bound theory depends heavily on how easy it is to verify the subexponential condition and how informative the resulting constants are. Proposition 5.4 shows existence of some beta under local exponential integrability, but this is fairly qualitative. As the conclusion acknowledges, obtaining usable bounds on beta remains open. So while the upper-bound framework is general, its operational value is somewhat limited unless one can instantiate it sharply in concrete model classes.

I also appreciate the attempt to connect the general upper bound to subsample-optimize methods. Corollary 6.1 gives a polylogarithmic coreset-size guarantee under subexponentiality, polynomial growth of Var_pi(ell), and an alignment condition on randomly sampled potentials relative to the residual approximation error. This is directionally important because it supports the empirical success of modern subsample-optimize approaches. That said, this result is also where the paper feels least complete. The alignment condition in Equation 27 is quite abstract and appears difficult to verify except case by case. In effect, the theorem says that if random subsampling repeatedly finds basis elements sufficiently aligned with the residual, then the method works. That is plausible, but it pushes much of the burden into an assumption that may encode the hard part of the problem. I do not think this invalidates the result, but it does limit how strongly one can interpret the claimed generality.

There are several points where the exposition could be improved for clarity and accessibility. First, the paper is dense with asymptotic notation and layered assumptions, and it is often difficult to keep track of which assumptions are model assumptions, which are data-generating assumptions, and which are algorithm-performance assumptions. A summary table would help substantially. For example, Assumption 3.2 is described as mild and typical of Bayesian asymptotics, but it bundles local Hessian convergence, score scaling, and concentration-rate requirements. Then Theorem 3.3 adds conditions on the coreset Hessian and score behavior, while Theorem 3.5 replaces some of these with smooth-below and lower-curvature assumptions. A compact roadmap of assumptions and implications would make the paper much easier to evaluate and use.

Second, the notation around the total coreset weight is hard to parse in the provided text, likely due to rendering issues, but even in the original manuscript I suspect this quantity should be given a simpler symbol and discussed more explicitly. Since many of the lower bounds depend on the sum of weights, it would help to explain early on why this quantity is central and how it behaves for different algorithms. Similarly, the use of min of forward/reverse KL for lower bounds and max of forward/reverse KL for upper bounds is mathematically understandable, but the practical interpretation deserves more discussion. In applications, forward and reverse KL can behave very differently, especially for multimodal or heavy-tailed targets. Some commentary on when the min-based lower bounds are strong enough to imply practically meaningful failure would be useful.

Third, while the experiments are aligned with the theory, they are somewhat limited in scope. The two synthetic examples are appropriate stress tests, but the empirical section mainly confirms asymptotic scaling trends already predicted by the theory. I would have liked at least one more experiment on a more standard benchmark model where previous theory does not apply cleanly but practitioners might care about actual runtime-quality tradeoffs. Also, the implementation details for Algorithm 3 matter a lot: the paper says weights were optimized by nonnegative least squares on discretized log-likelihoods using posterior samples. This is not exactly the optimization problem stated in Algorithm 3, which is KL minimization over the selected support. The approximation gap between the implemented surrogate objective and the theorem’s idealized objective should be discussed more explicitly.

On the technical side, I have a few concerns or requests for clarification.

One concern is the extent to which the lower-bound assumptions truly avoid restrictive posterior regularity. The paper emphasizes applicability to multimodal and heavy-tailed settings, which is fair globally, but Theorems 3.3 and 3.5 still rely on posterior concentration around a point theta_0 in a local Euclidean parameterization, with local quadratic behavior governed by H. This is weaker than global log-concavity, but it is still a local Bernstein–von Mises style regime around one concentration point. In multimodal settings, it would help to clarify whether theta_0 is intended to be one mode among several symmetric modes, whether the posterior mass outside B can still be negligible, and how the theory behaves when multiple separated regions retain nonvanishing posterior mass asymptotically. The examples suggest some robustness, but the general statements could be more precise about this.

A related issue is that the lower bounds are phrased in terms of a concentration set B with -log pi(B^c) entering the bound. This is elegant, but in practice the usefulness of the bound depends on choosing B so that local approximations are valid and posterior mass outside B is exponentially small enough. It would strengthen the paper to provide one or two worked examples showing how to choose r and verify the assumptions in detail, beyond the high-level conditions listed in Section 4. As written, the theory is plausible but somewhat abstract.

For Corollary 4.3, the statement that any coreset construction requires M > d to keep KL bounded is intuitively appealing and important. However, the assumptions (especially the linear independence and moment condition involving 1^T (G^T G)^(-1) 1) are fairly technical. I would like more intuition for when these conditions hold generically and whether they can fail in common models. Since this is presented as a fundamental limitation, readers will want to know how universal it really is. Is the result essentially a Carathéodory-type dimensional obstruction in disguise, or does it rely more delicately on random score geometry?

For the upper bounds, Definition 5.2 is broad, but perhaps too broad to be immediately interpretable. The paper would benefit from more examples of models satisfying A-subexponentiality, especially outside log-concave settings. Proposition 5.4 gives an existence result under local finiteness of the mgf around the origin, but this condition itself may fail in heavy-tailed posterior settings depending on the log-likelihood tails under pi. Since one of the paper’s selling points is heavy-tailed applicability, it would be useful to discuss more concretely why the two experimental models satisfy the needed integrability conditions for the upper-bound analysis.

I also think the computational desiderata in Section 2 deserve a bit more nuance. The paper requires coreset construction to run in o(N) time and memory, or at most O(N) with a small constant, and to produce M=o(N) with O(1) KL. This is a reasonable asymptotic idealization, but some of the analyzed methods, especially subsample-optimize approaches, may require posterior sampling or optimization steps whose cost depends nontrivially on M, dimension, and approximation machinery. Since the paper’s main claims are asymptotic and statistical rather than end-to-end computational, I would suggest softening or better justifying these desiderata.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution. The negative results are particularly strong and likely to influence how researchers think about coreset construction. The positive results are more assumption-laden, but still useful as a framework for analyzing modern methods beyond classical regular models. The paper’s ambition and breadth are commendable, and the technical development appears substantial.

My main suggestions for improvement are as follows. First, add a concise assumptions/results roadmap, ideally a table summarizing each theorem, its assumptions, and the kind of models/algorithms it covers. Second, expand the discussion around the alignment assumption in Corollary 6.1, including examples where it is expected to hold and where it may fail. Third, clarify the gap between the idealized optimization in Algorithm 3 and the practical implementation used in experiments. Fourth, provide more intuition and perhaps a short proof sketch for the key lower-bound results, especially how the local Gaussian approximation and score mismatch translate into KL growth rates. Fifth, discuss more explicitly the scope of the multimodal/heavy-tailed claims, especially when posterior mass does not asymptotically concentrate near a single local parameter value.

In summary, this is a strong theory paper with novel lower bounds, useful insights into the failure of importance-weighted coresets, and a promising general upper-bound framework. Its main weaknesses are that some assumptions, especially on the positive-results side, are abstract and difficult to verify, and that the exposition could do more to guide the reader through the technical landscape. Subject to those caveats, I view the work positively.

My recommendation is weak accept to accept, depending on the conference bar and the strength of the appendix proofs. The lower-bound contributions alone are quite valuable, and the paper advances the theoretical foundations of Bayesian coresets in a nontrivial way.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies theoretical guarantees for Bayesian coresets in a broad setting. It derives general asymptotic lower bounds on forward/reverse KL divergence between the full posterior and a coreset posterior under mild local regularity and concentration assumptions, and derives a general upper bound under a multivariate subexponentiality condition on centered log-likelihood contributions. These results are then used to show negative results for importance-weighted subsampling coresets—requiring coreset size proportional to dataset size to keep KL bounded, even after optimal global rescaling—and positive results for subsample-optimize methods, which can achieve bounded KL with polylogarithmic coreset size under additional alignment and variance-growth assumptions. The theory is illustrated on synthetic heavy-tailed, multimodal, and unidentifiable models that fall outside prior analyses based on exponential families or strong log-concavity.
strengths: Addresses an important gap in the Bayesian coreset literature by providing both lower and upper KL bounds beyond exponential-family and strongly log-concave settings.

The lower-bound framework is conceptually strong: it isolates local posterior concentration behavior and connects coreset quality to mismatch in gradients and aggregate weights, yielding interpretable impossibility results.
The negative result for importance-weighted coresets is significant and practically relevant; it offers a convincing theoretical explanation for previously observed poor empirical performance.
The upper-bound framework via generalized subexponentiality is reasonably broad and potentially applicable to heavy-tailed or nonstandard posteriors where prior theory does not apply.
The paper derives concrete corollaries for specific algorithm classes, not just abstract bounds, increasing practical relevance.
Empirical examples are well chosen to stress-test assumptions commonly used in prior work (multimodality, unidentifiability, heavy tails).
The presentation of the main contributions is clear at a high level, and the paper positions itself well relative to prior coreset theory.
weaknesses: Several key assumptions in the positive results are difficult to verify in practice, especially the subexponentiality constant in Proposition 5.4 and the alignment probability condition in Corollary 6.1; this limits operational usefulness of the upper bounds.
The empirical validation is narrow: only two synthetic models are considered, with no real-data experiments and limited comparison to a broader range of coreset construction baselines.

The practical algorithm analyzed in experiments for subsample-optimize uses an approximate weight optimization procedure (nonnegative least squares on discretized log-likelihoods) rather than the exact KL minimization stated in Algorithm 3, weakening the direct empirical validation of the theorem.
The asymptotic nature of the results leaves unclear how informative the bounds are at realistic finite sample sizes; finite-sample constants and tightness are not characterized.

The lower bounds focus on KL divergence and local concentration around a point; while broad, this may still miss settings where posterior mass is distributed across multiple separated regions without a dominant concentration point.

Some assumptions appear tailored to recover asymptotic normal-like local behavior despite the paper’s emphasis on nonstandard posteriors, so the true breadth of applicability may be narrower than suggested.
The paper does not provide constructive guidance for choosing sampling probabilities or verifying when the subsample-optimize assumptions hold in common model classes.
methodological_flaws: A notable scientific gap is the reliance of Corollary 6.1 on the alignment condition in Eq. (27), which is essentially an algorithm-dependent success assumption. Because this condition is not derived from more primitive model/data assumptions, the positive result is partly conditional on the algorithm already behaving well, reducing explanatory strength.

Proposition 5.4 asserts existence of a subexponential constant beta from local finiteness of exponential moments around the origin, but without the proof text it is hard to assess whether the conclusion is quantitatively meaningful; as stated in the main text it is existential and may be too weak to support practical guarantees.

The empirical section does not directly validate the assumptions underlying the theorems (e.g., concentration rates, subexponentiality, alignment probabilities), so the experiments mainly illustrate consistency with predicted trends rather than substantiate the theoretical mechanisms.

Algorithm 3 is analyzed as exact constrained KL minimization over sampled support, but the experiments replace this with a surrogate optimization based on posterior samples and discretized log-likelihoods. This creates a mismatch between theorem and experiment that weakens empirical validity.

The impossibility result for importance weighting depends on boundedness assumptions on sampling probabilities (Eq. 17). While reasonable, the paper argues performance would likely worsen outside this regime rather than proving it; thus the claimed generality of the negative conclusion is somewhat narrower than the narrative suggests.

The lower-bound theory depends on selecting a local neighborhood B around a concentration point theta_0 and on assumptions such as Hessian convergence to H. In genuinely multimodal settings with multiple comparable modes, the logic may only characterize one local region unless additional arguments establish dominant concentration or suitable pushforward structure.
